column3: Mary's own denial of unchastity directly precedes and answers the accusation framed in 19:28.
The townspeople's first public denunciation supplies the immediate setting for the kinship-based accusation.
Names mother and father as the closest ties, but in an eschatological rather than accusatory setting.
The ordering of a divine command does not clarify Mary, kinship, or the accusation.
Mary directs the accusers to the infant, initiating the narrative's answer to their charge.
Recognition of a brother after concealment loosely parallels the need to identify a person beyond an assumed public story.
Moses' sister and mother show family care, without addressing whether kinship proves moral character.
Jesus' declaration begins the direct vindication that follows the accusation against his mother.
Commands that kinship be named accurately and distinguishes mistaken from deliberate attribution, directly checking lineage-based claims.
Aaron as Moses' actual brother offers limited background for the kinship title in the focus ayah.
Jesus continues his self-description, extending the response that establishes his and Mary's standing.
The collective meaning of ummah does not illuminate the family accusation.
Moses' mother is a family reference without a relevant question of blame or reputation.
Jesus' stated devotion to his mother directly supplies the narrative's moral counterweight to the accusation.
Condemnation of calendar manipulation does not clarify the focus's family-based allegation.
Aaron's relationship to Moses gives only distant contextual resonance to the title "sister of Aaron."
Jesus' life-and-death declaration remains part of the immediate vindicating speech.
The return of evil upon those who expect it for others only generally resonates with wrongful condemnation.
The management of a command has no material connection to the focus.
This closing statement of the section provides narrative context but no specific light on the accusation.
Its prohibition of coercing women into prostitution sharply distinguishes sexual exploitation from an allegation of unchastity.
Rejecting a false account of Jesus' parentage continues the passage's correction of claims about Mary and her child.
Identifies Jesus truthfully as the son of Mary amid dispute, directly continuing her public vindication.
The rejected collective-identity reading does not support the focus's familial accusation.
Lot's wife remaining behind does not materially address kinship as evidence of individual guilt.
Jesus' public confession completes the immediate speech that answers the crowd's charge.
Shows that brotherhood is an ethical relation with duties, though it is not a claim about Mary's lineage.
Abraham's concern for his father preserves kinship across moral difference, but does not validate family reputation as proof.
The ensuing dispute is nearby narrative context without directly explaining the accusation.
Invoking forefathers in a resurrection objection illustrates ancestry as a rhetorical appeal, in a different issue.
Moses and Aaron's brotherhood is a limited parallel to the focus's kinship language.
The warning following the dispute stays in the same narrative sequence but does not bear on Mary's reputation.
The proper name Abu Lahab does not illuminate the focus's use of fatherhood or moral accusation.
Calls Lot's people a people of evil, providing a contrast between a warranted moral judgment and an imputed one.
The warning of regret is adjacent narrative context, not a treatment of Mary's alleged conduct.
Expiation of evil deeds concerns divine recompense rather than a public allegation based on family.
Moses' appeal to Aaron is a distant connection through the name only.
Demanding the return of ancestors concerns proof of resurrection, not personal reputation.
The rule about choice after a divine command does not clarify the focus.
The promise to the oppressed has no material relation to Mary's accusation.
The magicians' confession names the Lord of Aaron and Moses but adds no relevant kinship or blame logic.
Its defined family exceptions show that family terms can carry specific legal scope rather than general moral exoneration.
The contrast between evidence and beautified evil only generally cautions against distorted moral judgment.
Appeal to ancestors as demanded proof resembles faulty reliance on inherited association, but in a different debate.
Lot's household rescue does not materially illuminate the focus's accusation.
A prophet described as his people's brother illustrates social proximity, not Mary's individual standing.
Disagreement driven by wrongful rivalry does not clarify sexual accusation or family evidence.
The judgment on evildoers is too general to illuminate the focus.
Regulates speaking openly of evil and forgiving it, relevant to the public voicing of a serious moral allegation.
Shu'ayb as his people's brother offers only a general social use of kinship language.
The divine command is unrelated to the focus.
Shows how finding forefathers astray can become adopted moral inheritance, challenging ancestry as a reliable guide.
Public testimony clears Joseph of evil and exposes the actual wrongdoing, a close parallel to reputational vindication.
The brothers' attempt to persuade their father does not clarify the focus.
The witness-bearing community does not materially illuminate Mary's family accusation.
The consequences of an evil plot only generally contrast with the unproven charge in the focus.
Division from wrongful rivalry is not a useful neighbour for Mary's accusation.
The resurrection objection's mention of forefathers is too remote from the focus.
Collective disagreement after clear signs offers only a broad contrast with the passage's public dispute.
A community's appointed term does not illuminate the focus.
Formal allocation among parents and siblings distinguishes actual family relations but does not make them moral evidence.
Hūd as his people's brother gives only a generic social use of the term.
Division caused by wrongful rivalry does not materially clarify the focus.
The people's appeal to their fathers' practice exposes inherited association being used in place of justification.
The two women's reference to an elderly father supplies family context without a question of moral reputation.
Invoking Abraham as a shared father frames ancestry as a defined religious inheritance, not automatic proof of a person's conduct.
The flight from a brother shows kinship can fail under judgment, but it is remote from the focus.
Allows the wronged person to voice evil publicly, furnishing an ethical frame for allegation, defense, and justice.
Abraham questions his father and community's inherited worship rather than accepting family association as sufficient warrant.
The collective label "brothers of Lot" is unrelated to Mary's individual reputation.
Cain's murder of his brother shows that close kinship neither prevents nor determines individual wrongdoing.
The staged theft accusation involving a brother loosely parallels a public charge, but its narrative purpose differs.
Abraham disavows his father's and community's worship, directly showing that family connection need not define moral identity.
The possibility of replacing evil with good concerns repentance, not the basis of the focus's allegation.
The wish for final death does not illuminate the focus.
Rejects inherited ancestral practice as sufficient guidance, challenging the crowd's appeal to family standing as proof.
Moses' staff is unrelated to the focus.
Moses' prayer for himself and his brother shows kinship within shared accountability and mercy, not automatic innocence.
Abraham's question to his father and people tests inherited attachment rather than treating it as moral proof.
God's lordship over present people and forefathers relativizes ancestral authority and family prestige.
The queen's prior worship does not materially clarify the focus.
Rejects following forefathers merely because their path is inherited, a direct corrective to lineage-based reasoning.
Abraham's religious identity is not a useful neighbour for the specific accusation against Mary.
Opponents dismiss clear signs through what they have heard from forefathers, paralleling the use of inherited expectations to resist evidence.
The withholding of punishment while people seek forgiveness does not illuminate the focus.
Redirecting remembrance from fathers to God only broadly qualifies ancestor-centered attachment.
Moses' haste from his people is unrelated to the focus.
The mention of ancient ancestors warns that antiquity alone confers no authority, but the connection is limited.
Mary's election and purification provide direct prior testimony to the integrity challenged in 19:28.
Expiation through charity concerns forgiveness rather than the grounds of public accusation.
The complaint about food and ensuing disobedience do not clarify the focus.
Jacob evaluates a new promise by prior conduct, underscoring that trust should rest on deeds rather than kinship labels.
The denial of punishment is unrelated to the focus.
Metaphorical brotherhood with devils does not illuminate Mary's family accusation.
The reference to objects of worship is unrelated to the focus.
Divine acceptance and overlooking of sins concern individual moral assessment but not the public family-based charge.
Divine knowledge of what is disclosed or hidden does not materially clarify the focus.
The fellowship of devils in error is not a useful neighbour for Mary's accusation.
Fasting and piety are unrelated to the focus.
False claims of brotherhood show that a kinship-like label must be tested by conduct, though this is only a distant parallel.
Explicitly identifies the charge against Mary as a tremendous slander, making it the Qur'an's clearest direct counterpart to 19:28.
Condemns casting a sin upon an innocent person as slander and manifest wrongdoing, directly governing false moral accusation.
Names Jesus as the Messiah, son of Mary, while rejecting false claims about him; it clarifies his identity after the accusation scene.
Calls Mary a woman of truth, directly corroborating the integrity challenged in 19:28.
Jesus speaking from the cradle supplies a parallel attestation to the miraculous response that follows the focus ayah.
Begins Mary's maternal and family context with her consecration to God, which frames the lineage invoked in the accusation.
Mary's mother names her and asks divine protection for her and her offspring, directly establishing her protected family setting.
Mary's upbringing under Zechariah and extraordinary provision attest to her standing before the later public charge.
The dispute over Mary's guardianship establishes her public familial context but does not bear directly on the accusation.
The annunciation identifies the coming child as Jesus, son of Mary, providing direct prehistory for the contested birth.
Foretells Jesus speaking in the cradle, precisely anticipating the mode of vindication initiated after 19:28.
Mary states that no man has touched her; the angel explains the divine creation, directly answering the premise of the accusation.
Jesus' commissioned signs confirm the divine origin of his mission, though not the accusation's specific terms.
Introduces Mary's withdrawal from her family, the immediate narrative beginning of the events misread by her people.
The angel's appearance as a well-formed man explains the potentially misleading encounter behind the later accusation.
Mary seeks refuge from the apparent man, directly displaying the chastity and piety the crowd disregards.
The angel announces the gift of a pure son, establishing the divine rather than illicit origin of the pregnancy.
God declares the birth decreed and a sign and mercy, directly reframing what the crowd treats as disgrace.
Mary's conception and withdrawal explain the visible circumstance from which the public suspicion arises.
Her distress in labor gives the human cost of the pregnancy before the community's accusation.
The divine reassurance at childbirth continues the narrative evidence against interpreting Mary's condition as abandonment or guilt.
The provision and instruction at childbirth support the divinely ordered setting, though indirectly.
Mary's commanded vow of silence explains why she directs the accusers to the infant rather than defending herself verbally.
States that Mary guarded her chastity and that God breathed into her, a direct Qur'anic correction of the accusation.
Makes Mary and her son a sign, directly reframing their unusual situation as divine evidence rather than moral scandal.
Requires four witnesses for accusing chaste women and brands unsupported accusers as false, providing the governing evidentiary standard.
Allows reform after the punishment for unsupported sexual accusation, underscoring the gravity of making such claims.
Defines the public slander episode as a falsehood rather than a basis for treating an accused person's reputation as settled.
Requires believers to presume good of one another and identify an unsupported allegation as clear slander.
Reiterates the four-witness requirement, directly exposing the insufficiency of the crowd's family-based inference.
Warns that spreading an unproven accusation brings severe consequence, matching the focus's public shame dynamic.
Condemns passing along claims without knowledge and treating a grave matter as trivial.
Models the required response to scandalous hearsay: refusing to repeat it and declaring it a grave slander.
Warns believers never to return to such slander, reinforcing the ethical prohibition on the accusation's circulation.
States that God clarifies signs and rulings, supporting the legal-ethical frame for evaluating accusations.
Condemns those who want sexual immorality to spread as talk among believers, directly relevant to public sexual stigma.
Attributes protection from such wrongdoing to divine grace and mercy, a supporting rather than direct parallel.
Pronounces severe judgment on those who accuse chaste, unsuspecting believing women, directly matching the charge's form.
Contrasts corrupt and good speech and affirms that the good are innocent of what slanderers say, providing a vindication principle.
Condemns harming believing men and women with what they did not earn as slander and manifest sin.
Names Mary, daughter of Imran, as one who guarded her chastity and received God's spirit, directly resolving both lineage and conduct.
